lesson_title: Squares, Cubes and Roots of Fractions
hook_text: Why does squaring make this number smaller?
clip_script:
Let us build a square garden bed with sides two thirds of a metre. What is its area? Area of a square is side times side, so two thirds times two thirds. Picture a one-metre square, cut into thirds both ways: nine small squares, each one ninth of a square metre. Your bed covers two by two of them, four small squares. Four ninths of a square metre. Two thirds squared is four ninths, and you can see every one of the nine squares.

Now notice something odd. The side was two thirds of a metre, and the area is four ninths of a square metre, which is less than two thirds. Squaring made the number smaller. Why? Because the bed is less than a metre each way, so it covers less than two thirds of a one-metre strip — it is two thirds of a strip that is itself only two thirds of the big square. Part of a part.
visual_style: Top-down grid of a one-metre square shaded into ninths; a cube splitting into eight small cubes
pacing: slow reveal of the grid, then quick confirmations
